claim: The wtf meiotic driver gene family has persisted for over 100 million years.
source: The wtf meiotic driver gene family has unexpectedly persisted for over 100 million years
evidence: The title explicitly states the main finding of the manuscript, which is supported by phylogenetic and synteny analyses presented throughout the paper.

claim: Meiotic drivers bias their own transmission into more than half of the viable progeny produced by a driver+/driver− heterozygote.
source: Meiotic drivers are selfish elements that bias their own transmission into more than half of the viable progeny produced by a driver+/driver− heterozygote.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about meiotic drivers that is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Meiotic drivers are thought to exist for relatively short evolutionary timespans.
source: Meiotic drivers are thought to exist for relatively short evolutionary timespans because a driver gene or gene family is often found in a single species or in a group of very closely related species.
evidence: This statement reflects the prevailing theoretical expectation in the field prior to this study.

claim: wtf genes were identified in S. octosporus, S. osmophilus, and S. cryophilus.
source: We identify homologous genes in three other fission yeast species, S. octosporus, S. osmophilus, and S. cryophilus, which are estimated to have diverged over 100 million years ago from the S. pombe lineage.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by PSI-BLAST and BLASTn searches described in the methods and results.

claim: S. octosporus, S. osmophilus, and S. cryophilus diverged over 100 million years ago from the S. pombe lineage.
source: We identify homologous genes in three other fission yeast species, S. octosporus, S. osmophilus, and S. cryophilus, which are estimated to have diverged over 100 million years ago from the S. pombe lineage.
evidence: This divergence time is cited from published phylogenetic studies.

claim: Synteny evidence supports that wtf genes were present in the common ancestor of S. pombe, S. octosporus, S. osmophilus, and S. cryophilus.
source: Synteny evidence supports that wtf genes were present in the common ancestor of these four species.
evidence: The abstract states this conclusion, which is supported by detailed synteny analyses in Figure 4 and related text.

claim: wtf genes in S. octosporus cause meiotic drive.
source: Moreover, the ancestral genes were likely drivers as wtf genes in S. octosporus cause meiotic drive.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally through octad dissection analysis shown in Figures 8-10.

claim: Meiotic drive systems can be maintained for long evolutionary timespans.
source: Our findings indicate that meiotic drive systems can be maintained for long evolutionary timespans.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, inferred from the combined evidence of ancient origin and continued drive activity.

claim: During meiosis, the two alleles at a given locus segregate from each other and are each transmitted into an equal number of the viable gametes produced by a heterozygous organism.
source: During meiosis, the two alleles at a given locus segregate from each other and are each transmitted into an equal number of the viable gametes produced by a heterozygous organism. This fundamental rule of genetics is known as Mendel's law of segregation (Abbott and Fairbanks, 2016).
evidence: This is a fundamental principle of genetics supported by citation.

claim: Meiotic drivers are transmitted to most or even all of the functional gametes rather than 50% in a driver+/driver− heterozygote.
source: Rather than being transmitted to 50% of the gametes produced by a driver+/driver− heterozygote, meiotic drivers are transmitted to most or even all of the functional gametes (Sandler and Novitski, 1957; Zimmering et al., 1970).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to foundational work on meiotic drive.

claim: Meiotic drivers are found in diverse eukaryotes including plants, fungi, and animals.
source: Meiotic drivers are found in diverse eukaryotes including plants, fungi, and animals (Bravo Núñez et al., 2018b; Burt and Trivers, 2006; Courret et al., 2019a; Lindholm et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to review and research articles.

claim: Drivers in different systems are not thought to share common evolutionary origins.
source: Despite their broad phylogenetic distribution, drivers in different systems are not thought to share common evolutionary origins.
evidence: This reflects the prevailing view in the field based on theoretical considerations.

claim: Drivers are believed to have been born repeatedly, but each driver can only persist for a short evolutionary period before extinction.
source: Specifically, drivers are believed to have been born repeatedly, but each driver can only persist for a short evolutionary period before extinction, and as a result, drive systems are lineage-specific (Hatcher, 2000; Price et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a theoretical expectation supported by citations.

claim: Drive is generally costly to fitness.
source: Drive is generally costly to fitness.
evidence: This is a general principle in the field of meiotic drive.

claim: Some drivers act by destroying gametes that do not inherit them.
source: For example, some drivers act by destroying gametes that do not inherit them (Bravo Núñez et al., 2018b).
evidence: This mechanism is supported by citation to research on wtf drivers.

claim: Natural selection is thought to favor the evolution of drive suppressors.
source: Because of these costs, natural selection is thought to favor the evolution of drive suppressors (Cazemajor et al., 1997; Crow, 1991; Finseth et al., 2021; Kumon et al., 2021; Veller, 2022).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction supported by multiple citations.

claim: Suppressed drivers have no transmission advantage and are expected to accumulate inactivating mutations.
source: Suppressed drivers have no transmission advantage and are expected to accumulate inactivating mutations (Burt and Trivers, 2006).
evidence: This is a theoretical expectation supported by citation.

claim: A driver gene or gene family is often only found in a single species.
source: The molecularly identified meiotic drivers largely support the idea that drivers have limited evolutionary lifespans and confined species distributions, with a driver gene or gene family often only found in a single species (Finseth et al., 2021; Lindholm et al., 2016; Lyon, 2003; Price et al., 2019; Zanders and Johannesson, 2021).
evidence: This observation is supported by multiple citations to review articles.

claim: Drosophila melanogaster and D. simulans shared a common ancestor 5.4 million years ago.
source: In Drosophila, for example, the sister species Drosophila melanogaster and D. simulans shared a common ancestor 5.4 million years ago (Tamura et al., 2003), but they each contain distinct meiotic drive systems (Cazemajor et al., 1997; Helleu et al., 2016; Larracuente and Presgraves, 2012; Lin et al., 2018; Tao et al., 2007).
evidence: This divergence time is cited from a published phylogenetic study.

claim: D. melanogaster and D. simulans each contain distinct meiotic drive systems.
source: In Drosophila, for example, the sister species Drosophila melanogaster and D. simulans shared a common ancestor 5.4 million years ago (Tamura et al., 2003), but they each contain distinct meiotic drive systems (Cazemajor et al., 1997; Helleu et al., 2016; Larracuente and Presgraves, 2012; Lin et al., 2018; Tao et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to research on Drosophila drive systems.

claim: Sequences homologous to the Dox driver of D. simulans are found in D. mauritiana and D. sechellia.
source: For example, sequences homologous to the Dox driver of D. simulans are also found in D. mauritiana and D. sechellia (Muirhead and Presgraves, 2021; Vedanayagam et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent research on Dox.

claim: Sequences homologous to Dox appear to have existed 0.2 million years ago in the ancestor of the D. simulans clade.
source: Although there have been more recent introgressions involving Dox between D. simulans and D. mauritiana, sequences homologous to Dox appear to have existed 0.2 million years ago in the ancestor of the D. simulans clade (Meiklejohn et al., 2018; Muirhead and Presgraves, 2021; Vedanayagam et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to phylogenetic analyses of Dox.

claim: wtf driver genes are found in all sequenced isolates of S. pombe.
source: wtf driver genes are found in all sequenced isolates of the fission yeast S. pombe.
evidence: This is supported by previous genomic analyses cited in the text.

claim: Each sequenced S. pombe isolate contains between 4 and 14 distinct predicted wtf driver genes.
source: Each sequenced S. pombe isolate contains between 4 and 14 distinct predicted wtf driver genes (Eickbush et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous genomic studies.

claim: wtf drivers act by destroying the meiotic products (spores) that do not inherit the wtf driver from a wtf+/wtf− heterozygote.
source: The wtf drivers are killer meiotic drivers as they act by destroying the meiotic products (spores) that do not inherit the wtf driver from a wtf+/wtf− heterozygote (Figure 1A).
evidence: This mechanism is illustrated in Figure 1A and supported by previous research.

claim: Each wtf drive gene employs a poison protein and an antidote protein produced from two overlapping transcripts.
source: To cause selective spore death, each wtf drive gene employs a poison protein and an antidote protein produced from two overlapping transcripts.
evidence: This mechanism is supported by multiple citations to previous research on wtf genes.

claim: All developing spores are exposed to the poison, while only spores that inherit the wtf driver gene express the antidote and are rescued from destruction.
source: All developing spores are exposed to the poison, while only spores that inherit the wtf driver gene express the antidote and are rescued from destruction (Bravo Núñez et al., 2018a; Bravo Núñez et al., 2020a; Bravo Núñez et al., 2020b; Hu et al., 2017; Nuckolls et al., 2017).
evidence: This mechanism is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: 48 predicted wtf genes and 35 predicted wtf pseudogenes were identified in S. octosporus.
source: Overall, we identified 48 predicted wtf genes and 35 predicted wtf pseudogenes in S. octosporus; 31 predicted wtf genes and 11 predicted wtf pseudogenes in S. osmophilus; and 2 predicted wtf genes and 3 predicted wtf pseudogenes in S. cryophilus (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 1b-d).
evidence: This is based on PSI-BLAST and BLASTn searches described in the methods.

claim: 31 predicted wtf genes and 11 predicted wtf pseudogenes were identified in S. osmophilus.
source: Overall, we identified 48 predicted wtf genes and 35 predicted wtf pseudogenes in S. octosporus; 31 predicted wtf genes and 11 predicted wtf pseudogenes in S. osmophilus; and 2 predicted wtf genes and 3 predicted wtf pseudogenes in S. cryophilus (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 1b-d).
evidence: This is based on PSI-BLAST and BLASTn searches described in the methods.

claim: 2 predicted wtf genes and 3 predicted wtf pseudogenes were identified in S. cryophilus.
source: Overall, we identified 48 predicted wtf genes and 35 predicted wtf pseudogenes in S. octosporus; 31 predicted wtf genes and 11 predicted wtf pseudogenes in S. osmophilus; and 2 predicted wtf genes and 3 predicted wtf pseudogenes in S. cryophilus (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 1b-d).
evidence: This is based on PSI-BLAST and BLASTn searches described in the methods.

claim: 16 intact wtf genes and 9 pseudogenes were previously described in the reference isolate of S. pombe.
source: Previously, 16 intact wtf genes and 9 pseudogenes were described in the reference isolate of S. pombe (Bowen et al., 2003; Eickbush et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous genomic studies.

claim: The homology between the S. pombe wtf genes and those found in the other Schizosaccharomyces species is low.
source: The homology between the S. pombe wtf genes and those found in the other Schizosaccharomyces species is low (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequence identity analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The most similar wtf gene pair between S. pombe (FY29033 wtf25) and S. octosporus (S. octosporus wtf56) shares only 16% amino acid identity.
source: For example, the most similar wtf gene pair between S. pombe (FY29033 wtf25) and S. octosporus (S. octosporus wtf56) shares only 16% amino acid identity, compared to an average of 65.3% amino acid identity between orthologous gene pairs (Supplementary file 1a and e).
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison data presented in supplementary files.

claim: The overall gene structure of the candidate wtf genes in S. octosporus, S. osmophilus, and S. cryophilus is similar to the 5-exon wtf drivers and 5-exon wtf suppressors in S. pombe.
source: We found that the overall gene structure of the candidate wtf genes in S. octosporus, S. osmophilus, and S. cryophilus was similar to the 5-exon wtf drivers and 5-exon wtf suppressors in S. pombe (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by gene structure comparison shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The relative sizes of the corresponding exons and introns are remarkably similar between the species.
source: Moreover, the relative sizes of the corresponding exons and introns are remarkably similar between the species, even though the actual sequences are generally quite different (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequence alignment data.

claim: The FLEX motif is highly conserved in S. pombe, S. octosporus, S. osmophilus, and S. cryophilus.
source: Manual inspection of the MEME-discovered motifs revealed that the FLEX motif is highly conserved in these four species (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MEME analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: 20 of the 48 intact wtf candidate genes in S. octosporus possess confident FIMO hits in intron 1.
source: Inspecting intron 1 of the candidate wtf genes in the other three species showed that 20 of the 48 intact wtf candidate genes in S. octosporus possess confident FIMO hits in intron 1, 1 of the 2 intact wtf candidate genes in S. cryophilus possesses confident FIMO hits in intron 1, whereas none of the 31 intact wtf candidate genes in S. osmophilus possesses confident FIMO hits in intron 1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, Supplementary file 1b-d).
evidence: This is based on FIMO analysis of FLEX motif presence.

claim: 1 of the 2 intact wtf candidate genes in S. cryophilus possesses confident FIMO hits in intron 1.
source: Inspecting intron 1 of the candidate wtf genes in the other three species showed that 20 of the 48 intact wtf candidate genes in S. octosporus possess confident FIMO hits in intron 1, 1 of the 2 intact wtf candidate genes in S. cryophilus possesses confident FIMO hits in intron 1, whereas none of the 31 intact wtf candidate genes in S. osmophilus possesses confident FIMO hits in intron 1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, Supplementary file 1b-d).
evidence: This is based on FIMO analysis of FLEX motif presence.

claim: None of the 31 intact wtf candidate genes in S. osmophilus possesses confident FIMO hits in intron 1.
source: Inspecting intron 1 of the candidate wtf genes in the other three species showed that 20 of the 48 intact wtf candidate genes in S. octosporus possess confident FIMO hits in intron 1, 1 of the 2 intact wtf candidate genes in S. cryophilus possesses confident FIMO hits in intron 1, whereas none of the 31 intact wtf candidate genes in S. osmophilus possesses confident FIMO hits in intron 1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, Supplementary file 1b-d).
evidence: This is based on FIMO analysis of FLEX motif presence.

claim: All 48 intact S. octosporus wtf candidate genes have long transcripts initiating from upstream of exon 1.
source: All 48 intact S. octosporus wtf candidate genes have long transcripts initiating from upstream of exon 1, and 31 of them also have detectable short transcripts initiating from within intron 1 (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is based on long-read RNA sequencing data.

claim: 31 of the 48 intact S. octosporus wtf candidate genes have detectable short transcripts initiating from within intron 1.
source: All 48 intact S. octosporus wtf candidate genes have long transcripts initiating from upstream of exon 1, and 31 of them also have detectable short transcripts initiating from within intron 1 (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is based on long-read RNA sequencing data.

claim: The presence of the FLEX motif in intron 1 correlates with the expression of short transcripts in S. octosporus.
source: Thus, the presence of the FLEX motif in intron 1 correlates with the expression of short transcripts that likely correspond to the wtfpoison transcripts (p=0.016, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This correlation is demonstrated by statistical analysis of RNA-seq and FIMO data.

claim: Most of the wtf genes outside of S. pombe are closely associated with dispersed 5S rDNA genes.
source: Instead of a close association with transposon sequences, we found that most of the wtf genes outside of S. pombe are closely associated with dispersed 5S rDNA genes (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by genomic context analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: In S. octosporus, 87% (72/83) of wtf genes are associated with 5S rDNA genes.
source: In S. octosporus, S. osmophilus, and S. cryophilus, respectively, 87% (72/83), 79% (33/42), and 40% (2/5) of wtf genes are associated with 5S rDNA genes (Supplementary file 1j).
evidence: This is based on genomic annotation and analysis.

claim: In S. osmophilus, 79% (33/42) of wtf genes are associated with 5S rDNA genes.
source: In S. octosporus, S. osmophilus, and S. cryophilus, respectively, 87% (72/83), 79% (33/42), and 40% (2/5) of wtf genes are associated with 5S rDNA genes (Supplementary file 1j).
evidence: This is based on genomic annotation and analysis.

claim: In S. cryophilus, 40% (2/5) of wtf genes are associated with 5S rDNA genes.
source: In S. octosporus, S. osmophilus, and S. cryophilus, respectively, 87% (72/83), 79% (33/42), and 40% (2/5) of wtf genes are associated with 5S rDNA genes (Supplementary file 1j).
evidence: This is based on genomic annotation and analysis.

claim: In S. octosporus, S. osmophilus, and S. pombe, one or more wtf genes are present between the clr4 and met17 genes.
source: We found that in S. octosporus, S. osmophilus, and S. pombe, one or more wtf genes are present between the clr4 and met17 genes (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by synteny analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The gene trees of clr4 and met17 are consistent with the species trees.
source: We also reconstructed phylogenies of the fission yeast clr4 and met17 genes and found that the gene trees were consistent with the species trees (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: The ancestor of S. octosporus, S. osmophilus, S. cryophilus, and S. pombe had a wtf gene between clr4 and met17.
source: Together, our analyses are consistent with vertical transmission of clr4 and met17 and the wtf genes between them. This suggests the ancestor of S. octosporus, S. osmophilus, S. cryophilus, and S. pombe had a wtf gene between clr4 and met17 and that the wtf gene was lost in the lineage leading to S. cryophilus (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is inferred from synteny and phylogenetic analyses.

claim: The wtf gene between clr4 and met17 was lost in the lineage leading to S. cryophilus.
source: This suggests the ancestor of S. octosporus, S. osmophilus, S. cryophilus, and S. pombe had a wtf gene between clr4 and met17 and that the wtf gene was lost in the lineage leading to S. cryophilus (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is inferred from synteny analysis showing absence of wtf gene in S. cryophilus at this locus.

claim: S. pombe, S. octosporus, S. osmophilus, and S. cryophilus inherited wtf genes from a common ancestor with multiple wtf genes.
source: Altogether, our analyses indicate that S. pombe, S. octosporus, S. osmophilus, and S. cryophilus inherited wtf genes from a common ancestor with multiple wtf genes.
evidence: This is the conclusion from synteny and phylogenetic analyses.

claim: The S. pombe wtf genes are rapidly evolving.
source: Meiotic drivers are predicted to be rapidly evolving, and the S. pombe wtf genes support this prediction (Eickbush et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous evolutionary analyses.

claim: The rapid evolution of wtf genes is thought to be driven by genetic conflict between meiotic drivers and the rest of the genome.
source: This rapid evolution is thought to be driven by the genetic conflict predicted to exist between meiotic drivers and the rest of the genome.
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation based on evolutionary theory.

claim: In S. pombe, the evolutionary innovation of wtf genes stems from gene duplications, expansion, and contraction of tandem repeats within the coding sequences and extensive non-allelic gene conversion within the family.
source: In S. pombe, the evolutionary innovation of wtf genes stems from gene duplications, expansion, and contraction of tandem repeats within the coding sequences and extensive non-allelic gene conversion within the family (Eickbush et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous evolutionary analyses.

claim: The S. pombe wtf genes grouped together in a well-supported clade in a phylogenetic tree.
source: We observed that the S. pombe wtf genes grouped together in a well-supported clade (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: GARD detected evidence of non-allelic gene conversion within both S. octosporus and S. osmophilus wtf genes.
source: Consistent with the patterns described above, GARD detected evidence of non-allelic gene conversion within both S. octosporus and S. osmophilus (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by GARD analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Exon 4 of some wtf genes in S. octosporus and S. osmophilus encodes a 7 amino acid sequence that can be repeated in tandem multiple times.
source: We looked for amino acid repeats in our candidate wtf homologs and found a 7 amino acid sequence that was repeated a variable number of times in tandem in exon 4 of genes from S. octosporus and S. osmophilus.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of wtf genes.

claim: The repeat sequences in exon 4 are similar in S. pombe, S. octosporus, and S. osmophilus.
source: We found that the repeat sequences were similar in all three species, consistent with shared ancestry (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequence logo analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: In 83% (5 out of 6) of S. octosporus wtf loci without wtf genes in S. cryophilus and S. osmophilus, the S. cryophilus and S. osmophilus loci contain a 5S rDNA gene.
source: There are 6 such wtf loci. In 83% (5 out of 6) of those sites, the S. cryophilus and S. osmophilus loci contain a 5S rDNA gene (Supplementary file 1q and s).
evidence: This is based on synteny analysis of wtf and 5S rDNA loci.

claim: Expression of the Wtf4poison protein kills vegetative S. cerevisiae cells.
source: Expression of the Wtf4poison protein kills vegetative S. cerevisiae cells, and co-expression of the Wtf4antidote protein neutralizes the toxicity of the Wtf4poison protein.
evidence: This is based on previous research cited in the text.

claim: Co-expression of the Wtf4antidote protein neutralizes the toxicity of the Wtf4poison protein in S. cerevisiae.
source: Expression of the Wtf4poison protein kills vegetative S. cerevisiae cells, and co-expression of the Wtf4antidote protein neutralizes the toxicity of the Wtf4poison protein.
evidence: This is based on previous research cited in the text.

claim: Induction of each of the putative Wtfpoison proteins, except S. osmophilus wtf19, inhibited cell proliferation in S. cerevisiae.
source: We found that induction of each of the putative Wtfpoison proteins, except S. osmophilus wtf19, inhibited cell proliferation in S. cerevisiae (Figure 7A–C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by spot assay experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: The toxicity of each functional Wtfpoison protein was partially neutralized by co-expression of the cognate Wtfantidote proteins.
source: Moreover, the toxicity of each functional Wtfpoison protein was partially neutralized by co-expression of the cognate (i.e. encoded on the same gene) Wtfantidote proteins (Figure 7A–C; Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by spot assay experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: Wtfantidote proteins did not neutralize non-cognate Wtfpoison proteins.
source: Like our previous observations in S. pombe, we found that Wtfantidote proteins did not neutralize non-cognate Wtfpoison proteins (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A-E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by spot assay experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: S. octosporus Wtf25poison-GFP was distributed throughout the cytoplasm, with some potential endoplasmic reticulum localization.
source: S. octosporus Wtf25poison-GFP was distributed throughout the cytoplasm, with some potential endoplasmic reticulum localization, similar to what we previously observed for S. pombe Wtf4poison-GFP (Figure 7D, Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 7D.

claim: When S. octosporus Wtf25poison-GFP and Wtf25antidote-mCherry proteins were co-expressed, some colocalization of the proteins was observed.
source: When the S. octosporus Wtf25poison-GFP and Wtf25antidote-mCherry proteins were co-expressed, we observed some colocalization of the proteins (Figure 7F, Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Deletion of wtf25, wtf68, or wtf33 caused notable and significant spore viability reduction in heterozygous crosses.
source: In heterozygous crosses, deletion of wtf25, wtf68, or wtf33 caused notable and significant spore viability reduction (>5% spore viability reduction and p<0.05, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This is demonstrated by octad dissection analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: wtf+/wtf− heterozygotes for wtf25, wtf68, or wtf33 showed significant drive of the wild-type wtf+ allele among the viable spores.
source: These wtf+/wtf− heterozygotes also showed significant drive of the wild-type wtf+ allele among the viable spores (p<0.05, exact binomial test; Supplementary file 2b-d, Figures 8–9, Figure 9—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by octad dissection analysis shown in Figures 8-9.

claim: wtf25, wtf68, and wtf33 are active meiotic drivers.
source: These results indicate that wtf25, wtf68, and wtf33 are active meiotic drivers.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the octad dissection data showing drive.

claim: The levels of allele transmission bias favoring the wtf+ allele appear to be correlated with the expression levels of the poison isoform.
source: In fact, the levels of allele transmission bias favoring the wtf+ allele appear to be correlated with the expression levels of the poison isoform (Figure 9D).
evidence: This correlation is shown in Figure 9D comparing transmission distortion and poison expression.

claim: wtf25 integrated at the leu1 locus can act as a meiotic driver in a heterozygous cross.
source: Octad dissection analysis indicated that wtf25 integrated at the leu1 locus can act as a meiotic driver in a heterozygous cross (leu1Δ::wtf25/leu1), and the level of meiotic drive was comparable to that caused by the endogenous wtf25 gene (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by octad dissection analysis shown in Figure 10B.

claim: wtf25 can act in a locus-independent manner like the S. pombe wtf drivers.
source: This result indicates that S. octosporus wtf25 can act in a locus-independent manner like the S. pombe wtf drivers.
evidence: This is inferred from the ectopic integration experiment.

claim: The wtf25antidote-only allele was unable to kill spores not inheriting it in a wtf25 deletion background.
source: As expected, this allele was unable to kill spores not inheriting it in a wtf25 deletion background (Figure 10B, Supplementary file 2i).
evidence: This is demonstrated by octad dissection analysis shown in Figure 10B.

claim: The short transcript of wtf25 encodes a spore-killing poison.
source: This supports our hypothesis that the short transcript encodes a spore-killing poison.
evidence: This is inferred from the antidote-only mutant experiment.

claim: wtf25Δ spores that inherited the wtf25poison-only mutant allele at the leu1 locus were all inviable.
source: Among them, the wtf25Δ spores that also inherited the wtf25poison-only mutant allele at the leu1 locus were all inviable.
evidence: This is demonstrated by octad dissection analysis.

claim: The long isoform of wtf25 is required for protection against spore killing.
source: In addition, they demonstrate that the long isoform is required for protection against spore killing.
evidence: This is inferred from the poison-only mutant experiment.

claim: The wtf gene family is over 100 million years old.
source: Our analyses indicate that wtf genes were present in the common ancestor of S. octosporus, S. osmophilus, S. cryophilus, and S. pombe. As these species are estimated to have diverged ~119 million years ago (Rhind et al., 2011), we propose that the wtf gene family is over 100 million years old.
evidence: This is the main conclusion based on synteny and phylogenetic evidence combined with published divergence time estimates.

claim: Ancestral wtf genes could cause meiotic drive.
source: Our results suggest that ancestral wtf genes could cause meiotic drive, and we propose that wtf genes have at least occasionally caused meiotic drive throughout their history.
evidence: This is inferred from multiple lines of evidence including drive activity in S. octosporus and conserved gene features.

claim: The gene family exhibits several signatures of rapid evolutionary innovation typified by genes involved in genetic conflicts.
source: First, the gene family exhibits several signatures of the rapid evolutionary innovation typified by genes involved in genetic conflicts (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplements 1–3; Burt and Trivers, 2006; McLaughlin and Malik, 2017).
evidence: This is demonstrated by phylogenetic and sequence analyses shown in Figure 5.

claim: Genes from all four species encode both poison and antidote proteins, like the known drivers in S. pombe.
source: Also, genes from all four species encode both poison and antidote proteins, like the known drivers in S. pombe (Figure 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated by functional assays in S. cerevisiae shown in Figure 7.

claim: Genes from at least three species contain the FLEX regulatory motif upstream of the open reading frame that encodes a poison protein.
source: In addition, genes from at least three species contain the FLEX regulatory motif upstream of the open reading frame that encodes a poison protein, suggesting the genes are expressed in meiosis (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MEME and FIMO analyses shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Non-allelic recombination using repetitive 5S rDNA sequences has likely facilitated the expansion of the wtf gene family in S. octosporus and S. osmophilus.
source: In this study, we show that non-allelic recombination using repetitive 5S rDNA sequences has likely facilitated the expansion of the wtf gene family in S. octosporus and S. osmophilus.
evidence: This is inferred from synteny analyses showing wtf genes at sites with 5S rDNA in other species.

claim: The ancestor of S. octosporus, S. osmophilus, S. cryophilus, and S. pombe contained at least 2 wtf genes.
source: Our synteny analyses indicate that the ancestor of the four species contained at least 2 wtf genes (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1l), and the extant species carry between 5 and 83 wtf genes, including pseudogenes (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is inferred from synteny analyses shown in Figure 4.

claim: The extant species carry between 5 and 83 wtf genes, including pseudogenes.
source: Our synteny analyses indicate that the ancestor of the four species contained at least 2 wtf genes (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1l), and the extant species carry between 5 and 83 wtf genes, including pseudogenes (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on gene counts from genomic analyses shown in Figure 1B.

claim: wtf genes are compact and can autonomously cause drive.
source: The wtf genes are compact and can autonomously cause drive.
evidence: This is based on previous characterization of wtf genes and the ectopic integration experiment.

claim: A given Wtfantidote protein only neutralizes Wtfpoison proteins with amino acid sequences that are highly similar to that of the Wtfantidote.
source: Specifically, in all known cases, a given Wtfantidote protein only neutralizes Wtfpoison proteins with amino acid sequences that are highly similar to that of the Wtfantidote (Hu et al., 2017; Bravo Núñez et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on wtf protein specificity.

claim: Homotypic assembly underlies the Wtfpoison/Wtfantidote co-assembly that promotes neutralization of the poison by trafficking it to the vacuole.
source: This is likely because homotypic assembly underlies the Wtfpoison/Wtfantidote co-assembly that promotes neutralization of the poison by trafficking it to the vacuole (Nuckolls et al., 2020).
evidence: This mechanism is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Mutations in a wtf driver that generate a novel poison simultaneously generate a novel compatible antidote, as the two proteins are encoded on overlapping coding sequences.
source: Importantly, mutations in a wtf driver that generate a novel poison simultaneously generate a novel compatible antidote, as the two proteins are encoded on overlapping coding sequences.
evidence: This is inferred from the gene structure of wtf genes.

claim: Changes in intragenic repeat copy number are predicted to generate novel drivers and suppressors.
source: For example, changes in intragenic repeat copy number are predicted to generate novel drivers and suppressors (Bravo Núñez et al., 2018a, Nuckolls et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on wtf repeat regions.

claim: S. pombe genomes share >99% DNA sequence identity.
source: Despite S. pombe genomes sharing >99% DNA sequence identity (Jeffares et al., 2015), the wtf genes found in the four assembled isolates are generally distinct (Hu et al., 2017; Eickbush et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a genomic study.

claim: There is only one locus, wtf4, where all four S. pombe isolates contain a driver.
source: In fact, there is only one locus, wtf4, where all four isolates contain a driver (Eickbush et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous genomic analysis.

claim: The antidote from Sp wtf4 does not neutralize the poison from Sk wtf4 and vice versa.
source: Even the two most similar wtf4 drivers, from the reference genome (Sp) and the S. kambucha isolate (Sk), are distinct drivers in that the antidote from Sp wtf4 does not neutralize the poison from Sk wtf4 and vice versa (Nuckolls et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous functional analysis.
